reading.body:
NTT Chicago CH1 has 36 MW of published IT capacity, making it one of six Illinois data centers that disclose load figures and accounting for 15 percent of the state's total disclosed capacity.

Illinois maps 44 data center facilities but only six publish their power consumption. This transparency gap means 38 mapped sites remain invisible to grid planning. For a state trying to anticipate AI infrastructure demands, the absence of these numbers creates a blind spot. NTT's willingness to publish its capacity is unusual enough to be notable.

Whether NTT Chicago CH1 can actually handle large-scale AI training is unknowable from its published specifications. The facility discloses power draw but not electrical service rating, cooling capability, or grid qualifications. These constraints matter more than headline capacity for AI workloads, which pack 40 kW or more into single racks. A 36 MW facility could hold 900 racks at typical AI density, but only if the building's infrastructure supports it.

The data shows what one operator chose to tell the market, not what grid planners need to know. Illinois's capacity visibility problem is common. Without disclosure from all operators, forecasting power demand for AI infrastructure remains guesswork.
